steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Market segmentation divides the market into groups with similar characteristics: demographic (age, gender, income), geographic (location), psychographic (lifestyle, values), and behavioural (purchasing habits, brand loyalty).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Primary research collects new data directly: surveys, focus groups, interviews, observations. It's specific to the business but expensive and time-consuming.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Secondary research uses existing data: government statistics, trade reports, competitor accounts, internet research. It's cheaper and faster but may be outdated or not specific to the business's needs.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Quantitative data is numerical and statistical (percentages, averages, charts); qualitative data is descriptive (opinions, feelings, reasons behind choices). Both are valuable - quantitative shows WHAT, qualitative shows WHY.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Explain the difference between primary and secondary market research, giving two advantages of each. | Describe how market segmentation can help a business target its products more effectively. | Evaluate whether a business should rely more on primary or secondary research when launching a new product.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Primary research: collected first-hand for a specific purpose. Advantages: up-to-date, directly relevant, owned by the business (competitors can't access it). steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always specify the TYPE of segmentation: don't just say 'segmentation', say 'demographic segmentation by age'. When evaluating research, link back to DECISION-MAKING: how does the data help the business choose? Remember: primary = new data for a specific purpose; secondary = existing data from other sources.
